For a more in-depth treatments of the topic of regular variation, with specific focus on useful results we refer the reader to (Bingham et al. 1987) For statistical applications of regular variation, see (Nair et al. 2022; Emchrechts et al. 2012; de Haan and Ferrerira 2006). Many classical results applying this theory to probablity, particularly the arcsin distribution and applications to renewal theory can be found in Volume II of Feller (Feller 1971).

Preliminary Definitions

Definition 1 A function \(f : \R \rightarrow \R\) is regularly varying at \(\infty\) with exponent \(\alpha \in \R\), and write \(f \in \calR_\alpha^{\infty}\) if for all \(\lambda > 0\), \[ \begin{equation*} \lim_{x\uparrow\infty}\frac{f(\lambda x)}{f(x)} = \lambda^{\alpha}. \end{equation*} \]

Definition 2 A function \(\ell : \R \rightarrow \R\) is slowly varying at \(\infty\), and write \(\ell \in \calR_0^{\infty}\), if for all \(\lambda > 0\), \[ \begin{equation*} \lim_{x\uparrow\infty}\frac{\ell(\lambda x)}{\ell(x)} = 1. \end{equation*} \]

Definition 3 We call \(g : \R \rightarrow \R\) regularly varying at \(0\) with exponent \(\alpha \in \R\), and write \(g \in \calR_\alpha^{0}\) if for all \(\lambda > 0\), \[ \begin{equation*} \lim_{s\downarrow 0}\frac{g(\lambda s)}{g(s)} = \lambda^{\alpha}. \end{equation*} \]

Structurally, this is equivalent to a regularly varying function at infinity with reciprocal argument, i.e., \[ \begin{equation*} \lim_{s\downarrow 0}\frac{f\pr{\frac{1}{\lambda s}}}{f\pr{\frac{1}{s}}} = \lambda^{-\alpha} . \end{equation*} \] By construction, we can define any regularly varying function as the product of a slowly varying function \(\ell \in \calR_{0}^{\infty}\) and a power law part \(x^{\alpha} \in \calR_{\alpha}^{\infty}\). That is, if \(f \in \calR_{\alpha}^{\infty}\), we may write \[ \begin{equation*} f(x) = \ell(x) x^{\alpha}, \end{equation*} \] where \(\ell(x)\) is a suitably-chosen slowly varying function that captures deviation of \(f(x)\) from a pure power law \(\propto x^{\alpha}\) at finite values of \(x\).1 2

1 It is useful to consider slowly varying functions \(\ell(x)\) as sub-polynomial (Lemma 2.7 in Nair et al. 2022), where \[\begin{equation*} \lim_{x \uparrow \infty} \ell(x)x^{\rho} = \begin{cases} 0, \quad \rho < 0 \\ \infty, \quad \rho > 0. \end{cases} \end{equation*}\] Two simple examples of slowly varying functions are constants \(\ell(n) = C > 0\) and \(\ell(n) = \pr{\log n}^\gamma\) for any \(\gamma \in \R\).

2 It is also very important here to ask what this means with respect to regularly varying sequences \(f_n\). Here there is no burden, and we may just define \(f_n = (f_n/n^{\alpha})n^{\alpha} \doteq \ell(n) n^{\alpha}\), though we must restrict ourselves to \(n\in \Z_{+}\); for instance by taking the integer part \(f(x) =\ell([x])[x]^\alpha\). What however is interesting, is that we may go even further and consider a continuous argument \(x\in \R_+\) by defining a continuous function \(f(x)\) which agrees with \(f_n = f(n)\) on the integers, and otherwise has useful properties. For instance, for a regularly varying sequence \(f_n\) we can simply define \(f(x)\) as its smooth interpolation such that \(f([x]) = f_{[x]}\). This representation allow us to often ignore whether our regularly varying function is continuous or discrete, and derive general results.

Fundamental Theorems

The first of the “fundamental theorems of regular variation’’ (for derivatives) to be discussed is the Monotone Density Theorem (Theorem 2.11 in (Nair et al. 2022)). This and the accompanying theorem to follow (dealing with integrals; see Theorem 2.10 in (Nair et al. 2022) or Theorem A3.7 in (Emchrechts et al. 2012)) will be used frequently in our proofs to follow. The condition of eventual-monotonicity required for the Monotone Density theorem is in some cases difficult to check, but is essentially determined by the behavior of the slowly varying function \(\ell(\cdot)\). This condition is often evaluated with a secondary notions/conditions.3

3 In the context of probability distributions \(\Pr[X \le n]\), and in the discrete case their associated probability masses, two conditions that guarantee eventual monotonicity are (1) log-concavity of \(\mu_n = \Pr[X = n]\), i.e. \(\mu_n^2 \ge \mu_{n-1}\mu_{n+1}\) and (2) complete monotonicity where all \(k\)-fold finite differences \(\Delta^k\) of \(\mu_n\) are such that \((-1)^k \Delta^k \mu_n \ge 0\) for all \(k\ge 0\) and \(n\ge 0\). This second result is equivalent to being able to write \[\begin{equation*} \mu_n =\int_{0}^1 z^n\dd \nu (z) = \int_{0}^\infty e^{-sn}\dd \xi (s) \end{equation*}\] by the Hausdorff moment theorem (Hausdorff 1921) for Borel measures \(\nu\) and \(\xi\). For alternative conditions justifying the result of the Monotone Density Theorem, refer to Sections 1.6 and 1.7 of Bingham et al. (1987). For instance, we are able to argue that the Monotone Density Theorem applies (see (Bingham et al. 1987), Sec. 1.8.1, Proposition 1.8.2) so long as \(\mu_n\) is smoothly varying (guaranteed if \(\Pr[X > n] = \ell(n)n^{-\alpha}\) is smoothly varying).

Theorem 1 Let \(F \in \calR_{\alpha}^{\infty}\) and let \(\Delta F\) denote the derivative \(\Delta F(n) = F'(n)\), if \(F\) is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, and the finite difference operator \(\Delta F(n) = F(n)-F(n-1)\) if \(F\) is discrete. If \(\Delta [F]\) is eventually monotone in the sense that there exists an \(N\) such that for \(\Delta F(n)\) is monotone for \(n > N\), then \[ \begin{align*} n \Delta F (n) \sim \alpha F(n), \quad n > N, \end{align*} \] and therefore \(\Delta F \in \calR_{\alpha-1}^{\infty}\).

Proof. We consider the discrete case, which is not often seen, but whose proof is similar to the absolutely continuous case, where one needs only to substitute an integral whenever a sum appears below. Without loss of generality, assume that \(\Delta [F] (n)\) is non-decreasing for \(n > N\), and let $0 < a < b $; the non-increasing will be implied by changing the direction the following inequalities. By definition of \(F\), we can of course write \[ \begin{equation*} \sum_{i = [sn]}^{[tn]} \frac{\Delta [F] (n)}{F (n)} = \frac{F ([tn]) - F ([sn])}{F (n)}. \end{equation*} \] With $n > N / s $, by monotonicity we have \[ \begin{equation} \frac{\Delta [F] ([sn])([tn] - [sn])}{F(n)} \le \frac{F ([tn]) - F ([sn])}{F (n)} \le \frac{\Delta [F] ([tn])([tn] - [sn])}{F(n)} . \end{equation} \tag{1}\] By regular variation, as \(F \in \calR_{-\alpha}\), we may represent \(F(n) = \ell(n)n^{-\alpha}\). Considering only valid integer arguments we see \[ \begin{equation*} \lim_{n}\frac{F ([sn])}{F (n)} = \lim_{n}\frac{[sn]^{\alpha}\ell([sn])}{n^{\alpha}\ell(n)} = s^{\alpha}. \end{equation*} \] The ratio \(\lim_{n}[sn]/n = s\), is well known result, and therefore of course this implies that \(\lim_{n}\pr{[sn]/n}^{\alpha} = s^{\alpha}\). When \(\ell(\cdot)\) is eventually non-decreasing as supposed by eventual monotonicity of \(F(\cdot)\), then \[ \begin{align*} \frac{\ell(sn-1)}{\ell(n)} \le \frac{\ell([sn])}{\ell(n)} \le \frac{\ell(sn)}{\ell(n)} \rightarrow 1 \end{align*} \] the left side can be re-written and satisfies the same limit as the right expression in our string of inequalities \[ \begin{align*} \frac{\ell(sn-1)}{\ell(n)} = \frac{\ell((s-\frac{1}{n})n)}{\ell(n)} \rightarrow 1. \end{align*} \] If \(\ell(\cdot)\) is not continuous, but rather a discrete \(\ell_{[n]}\), as we will discuss later it is equivalent to define a new eventually monotone function which continuously interpolates \(\ell([n])=\ell_{[n]}\) and use it as a surrogate. Going back now to Equation 1, dividing all terms by \(n(t-s)\), consider the left most expression \[ \begin{equation*} \limsup_{n}\frac{n\Delta [F] ([sn]) }{F(n)}\frac{([tn] - [sn])}{n(t-s)}. \end{equation*} \] The second term in the product simply tends to \(1\) \[ \begin{equation*} \frac{([tn] - [sn])}{n(t-s)} \rightarrow 1, \end{equation*} \] so that in total \[ \begin{equation*} \limsup_{n}\frac{n \Delta [F] ([sn]) }{F(n)} \le \frac{t^{\alpha} - s^{\alpha}}{t-s} \end{equation*} \] By considering the right most expression in Equation Equation 1 we also have that \[ \begin{equation*} \liminf_{n}\frac{n\Delta [F] ([tn]) }{F(n)} \ge \frac{t^{\alpha} - s^{\alpha}}{t-s}. \end{equation*} \] where letting \(a=1\) (respectively \(b=1\)) and taking \(b\downarrow1\) (respectively \(a\uparrow1\)) gives the desired result that by squeeze \[ \begin{equation*} \lim_{n}\frac{n \Delta [F] (n) }{F(n)} = \alpha. \end{equation*} \]

Theorem 1 demonstrates that, far enough into the tail, the contribution of \(\Delta F\) to \(F\) can be estimated by simply taking the derivative of its power-law part. In the case of a probability distribution, this result indicates that when the tail is regularly varying, i.e., \(\Fbar(m) = \Pr[S_1 > m]=\ell(m)m^{-\alpha}\), then so long as its probability masses \(f_m\) are eventually-monotone decreasing, \(f_m \sim \alpha \ell(m) m^{-(1+\alpha)}\).

There are two important differences to highlight between the absolutely continuous case and the discrete case of Theorem 1. First is whether we express the original function \(F\) as an integral or a summation when considering the ratio \[ \begin{equation*} \sum_{i = [sn]}^{[tn]} \frac{\Delta F (n)}{F (n)} = \frac{F ([tn]) - F ([sn])}{F (n)}. \end{equation*} \] Second is whether \(\ell(\cdot)\) is continuous, rather discrete (i.e., \(\ell(n) = \ell_{[n]}\)). In the discrete case, as we will discuss later, it is equivalent to define a new eventually monotone function which smoothly interpolates \(\ell([n])=\ell_{[n]}\).

The complement to Theorem 1 is known as Karamata’s Integral Theorem. While the Monotone Density Theorem states that \(\Delta F(x) \sim \ell(x) \Delta(x^\alpha)\) as \(x\uparrow\infty\), Karamata’s Integral Theorem states that \(\int_0^y F(x)\dd x \sim \ell(y) \int_0^{y}x^\alpha \dd x\) as \(y\uparrow\infty\) (up to some dependence on \(\alpha\)). As this is no longer a point-wise result and instead requires integration over an interval, we will need the following theorem indicating the uniformity by which regular variation applies. A proof can be found in (de Haan and Ferrerira 2006), where this result appears as Theorem B.1.4.

Theorem 2 If \(f \in \calR_{\alpha}^{\infty}\) then there exists a \(t_0 \ge 0\) such that for any bounded and non-negative \(a\) and \(b\), \[ \begin{equation*} \frac{f(xt)}{f(x)} \rightarrow t^{\alpha}, \quad \text{uniformly over} \ t \in [a,b], \ t_0 \le a < b < \infty . \end{equation*} \]

Theorem 3 Let \(f \in \calR_{\alpha}^{\infty}\), then there exists a \(t_0 > 0\) such that, \[ \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \int_{t_0}^{t}f(y) \dd y &\sim \frac{1}{\alpha + 1}tf(t), \quad t \uparrow \infty \quad \alpha \ge -1, \\ \int_{t}^{\infty}f(y) \dd y &\sim \frac{-1}{(\alpha + 1)}tf(t), \quad t \uparrow \infty \quad \alpha < -1. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} \] That is, \(\int f(y) \dd y \in \calR_{\alpha + 1}^{\infty}\) for \(\alpha < 0\) and \(\alpha > 0\), respectively, over their valid intervals.

A proof of Theorem Theorem 3 can be found in the appendix of (de Haan and Ferrerira 2006)4, as Theorem B.1.5 (see also Theorem 2.10 in (Nair et al. 2022) or Theorem A3.7 in (Emchrechts et al. 2012)). The primary argument comes from applying the Uniform Convergence Theorem for regular varying functions after a change of variables \[ \begin{equation*} \frac{F(tx)-F(t)}{tf(t)} = \int_{1}^{x}\frac{f(tu)}{f(t)} \dd u \rightarrow \frac{x^{\alpha + 1}-1}{\alpha + 1}, \quad t \uparrow \infty. \end{equation*} \]

4 The idea presented in (de Haan and Ferrerira 2006) is to first show that these integrals are finite for finite intervals (locally bounded). Afterwards, by regular variation, one can show show that there exists a \(t_\varepsilon\) such that for \(t > t_\varepsilon\), \(f(xt) \le (1 + \varepsilon)x^{\alpha}f(t)\). For example as \(F(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} f(y) \dd y \uparrow \infty\) we can write for fixed \(x\) \[ \begin{equation*} \frac{F(tx)}{F(t)} = \frac{\int_{t_0}^{tx} f(y) \dd y}{\int_{t_0}^{t} f(y) \dd y} \sim \frac{\int_{t_\varepsilon x}^{tx} f(y) \dd y}{\int_{t_\varepsilon}^{t} f(y) \dd y} = \frac{x\int_{t_\varepsilon }^{t} f(xy) \dd y}{\int_{t_\varepsilon}^{t} f(y) \dd y} \le (1+2\varepsilon)x^{\alpha+1}, \quad t \uparrow \infty \end{equation*} \] where the \(2\varepsilon\) considers the adjustment needed for the middle and final approximation as well as the stated inequality. A lower limit is also found in the same manner (with lower bound coefficient \((1-2\varepsilon)\)). Thus by squeeze \(F(t) \in \calR_{\alpha + 1}\).

Extending this result to include integration over \([0,x]\) or \([x,\infty)\) for \(\alpha > -1\) and \(\alpha \le -1\), respectively, requires integrability of \(f\) over these regions so that the denominator \(tf(t)\) dominates \(\int f(s)\dd s\) over these regions.

Karamata’s Tauberian Theorem

Here we present one of the most important/foundation tools in this theory, the Karamata Tauberian Theorem (Theorem 6). Proofs of this result rely on Potter’s Bound, which relies on the following representation theorem.

Theorem 4 Let \(f \in \calR_{\alpha}^{\infty}\), and let \(F(x) = \int_{x_0}^{x}f(t) \dd t\) where for \(x > x_0\) \(f(x)\) is positive. Then there exists a function \(\lim_{x\uparrow\infty}c_0(x) = c_0 > 0\), such that \[ \begin{equation*} f(x) = c_0(x) b(x) \exp\pr{\int_{1}^{x} \frac{b(t) - 1}{t} \dd t}, \end{equation*} \] where \(b(x) = xf(x)/F(x)\) obeys \[ \begin{equation*} \lim_{x \uparrow \infty} b(x) = \begin{cases} -(\alpha + 1), \quad \alpha < -1 \\ \alpha + 1, \quad -1 \le \alpha . \end{cases} \end{equation*} \]

A proof of this can be found in (de Haan and Ferrerira 2006) as a remark related to the proof of Karamata’s Theorem, Theorem B.1.5. The case of discrete sequences is not obvious, but follows again by defining \(f(x)\) as a smooth interpolation such that \(f([x]) = f_{[x]}\), which by Theorem Theorem 4 will have a valid representation.5

5 Karamata’s Representation Theorem (Theorem B.1.6 in (de Haan and Ferrerira 2006)) has multiple equivalent representations, sometimes just written as \[ \begin{equation*} f(x) = c_1(x) \exp\pr{\int_{x_0}^{x} \frac{a(t)}{t} \dd t}, \end{equation*} \] where \(a: \R^{+} \rightarrow \R\) and \(c: \R^{+} \rightarrow \R\) are measurable functions such that again \(a(x) \rightarrow \alpha\) and \(c_1(x) \rightarrow c_1 > 0\).

The representation given in Theorem 4 is useful in bounding the error of \(f(xt)/f(t)\) compared to \(x^{\alpha}\) uniformly in \(x\), rather than just point-wise. Applying this representation and a change of variables, \[ \begin{equation*} \frac{f(xt)}{f(t)} = \frac{c_1(xt) }{c_1(t) } \exp\pr{\int_{t}^{xt} \frac{b(s) - 1}{s} \dd s} = \frac{c_1(xt) }{c_1(t) } \exp\pr{\int_{1}^{x} \frac{b(ts) - 1}{s} \dd s}. \end{equation*} \] By combining the Theorem 2 and Theorem 3, we have that for specified \(\delta_1,\delta_2>0\), we can ensure that \(|\frac{c_1(xt) }{c_1(t) } - 1| \le \delta_1\) and \(|b(ts)-1-\alpha| \le \delta_2\) for large enough \(t > t_0\) uniformly in \(s \ge \min\{1,x\}\). For arbitrary \(x > 0\), this gives us upper and lower bounds on the ratio, a result known as Potter’s Bound (see, e.g., Proposition B.4.1.5 in (de Haan and Ferrerira 2006)).

Theorem 5 Let \(f \in \calR_{\alpha}^{\infty}\) and let \(\delta_1, \delta_2 > 0\). There exists \(t_0 \in \R\) such that \[ \begin{equation*} (1-\delta_1) x^{\alpha} \min \{x^{-\delta_2},x^{\delta_2} \}\le \frac{f(xt)}{f(t)} \le (1+\delta_1) x^{\alpha} \max \{x^{-\delta_2},x^{\delta_2} \} \end{equation*} \] for all \(t \ge \max\{ t_0, t_0/x \}\).

Here, if we are considering the ratio \(g(x/t)/g(1/t)\) for a function \(g\) that is regular varying at \(0\) rather than at \(\infty\), the condition presented in the theorem would be in terms of inverse arguments \(s = t\) and \(y = 1/x\). The required relation per Potter’s Bound that \(s \ge \max\cbr{s_0, s_0/y}\), would here equate instead to \(t \ge \max\cbr{s_0,s_0x}\). We note therefore that for \(\theta \in [0,a]\) for some fixed \(a>0\), this condition can always be satisfied uniformly in \(\theta\) for large enough \(t\)

The discrete case of Theorem 5 is also true, and ensures the existence of \(n_0 = n_0(\delta_1,\delta_2)\) such that for \(n,m>n_0(\delta_1,\delta_2)\), \[ \begin{equation*} (1-\delta_1) (m/n)^{\alpha} \min \{(m/n)^{-\delta_2},(m/n)^{\delta_2} \}\le \frac{f_m}{f_n} \le (1+\delta_1) (m/n)^{\alpha} \max \{(m/n)^{-\delta_2},(m/n)^{\delta_2} \}, \end{equation*} \] with \(m/n\) the analogue of \(x\); for instance we could define \(m=[xn]\) for some \(x>0\).

Potter’s Bound is an important result in justifying dominated convergence any compact interval not containing values below \(t_0\). For example, Potter’s bound can be used to prove the following lemma (see Lemma B.1.12 in (de Haan and Ferrerira 2006)).

Lemma 1 Let \(f \in \calR_{\alpha}^{\infty}\) with \(\alpha > -1\) be Lebesgue integrable over finite intervals of \(\R_{+}\), and let \(k: \R_{+} \rightarrow \R\) be a measurable function such that there exists \(\varepsilon > 0\) where \[ \begin{equation*} \int_{0}^{1} x^{\alpha-\varepsilon} k(x) \dd x < \infty, \quad \int_{1}^{\infty} x^{\alpha+\varepsilon} k(x) \dd x < \infty . \end{equation*} \] Then \[ \begin{equation*} \lim_{t\uparrow \infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{f(xt)}{f(t)}k(x) \dd x = \int_{0}^{\infty}x^{\alpha}k(x) \dd x . \end{equation*} \]

Proof. The proof of Lemma 1 follows from Potter’s bound, which shows that dominated convergence holds for compact intervals, extended to \(\R_+\) so long as the integral is finite.
The only complicating part is the interval near \(0\). Here, one has that as \(f\) is integrable near \(0\) and \(k(\cdot)\) is bounded that \[ \begin{equation*} \abs{\int_{0}^{t_0/t}\frac{f(xt)}{f(t)}k(x) \dd x} \le \frac{1}{tf(t)}\int_{0}^{t_0}\abs{f(s)k\pr{\frac{s}{t}}} \dd s \downarrow 0 \end{equation*} \] as when \(\alpha > -1\), \(tf(t) \uparrow \infty\). Note that as long as \(1-\alpha - \varepsilon > 0\), \(t^{-\alpha - \varepsilon}k(t)\) is integrable on \((0,1)\). On the other end, we have by Potter’s bound i.e. \[ \begin{equation*} \frac{f(tx)}{f(t)} \le c x^{-\alpha \pm \varepsilon}, \quad tx \ge t_0, x \in \R_{+} \end{equation*} \] this implies in total by dominated convergence that \[ \begin{equation*} \int_{t_0/t}^{1}k(x) \frac{f(tx)}{f(t)}\dd x \rightarrow \int_{0}^{1}k(x) x^\alpha \dd x \end{equation*} \]

Theorem 6 is a combination of two results. The first replaces the traditional Karamata Tauberian Theorem with its Fourier equivalent, a result established by Garsia and Lamperti (Lemma 3.2.1 in (Garsia and Lamperti 1963); a straightforward application of Potter’s Bound 6). Garsia and Lamperti’s result will only apply, however, to distributions with regular varying tails \(\Pr[S_1>n]=\ell(n)n^{-\alpha}\) with infinite mean, i.e., where \(\alpha \in (0,1)\). The second result extends this result to \(\alpha>1\), the case where \(S_1\) has finite mean (see, for example, Theorem 2.16 in (Nair et al. 2022)). The proof of this result follows by analyzing iterated integrals of a regularly varying function through repeated integration-by-parts. Alternatively, this can be observed via Taylor expansion of \(\int_0^\infty e^{-st} \dd F(t)\) which is non-decreasing (actually completely monotone) and absolutely continuous in \(s\).

6 Though we recommend just checking the paper, we briefly account the analysis. First they consider an integration by parts applied to \[ \begin{equation*} 1-\Phi(\theta) = \int_{0}^{\infty}(1-e^{i\theta x})\dd \mu(x), \end{equation*} \] so that this expression can be written in terms of \(\Fbar(x)\) which is assumed to be regularly varying. In this context Potter’s Bound indicates still applies, where per Garsia and Lamperti (Garsia and Lamperti 1963): there exists a \(\lambda(\varepsilon) > 0\) for a chosen small \(\varepsilon>0\) such that such that for all \(\sigma\) with \(\theta\lambda(\varepsilon)\le \sigma \le 1\) \[ \begin{equation*} \frac{\Fbar(\sigma/\theta)}{\Fbar(1/\theta)} \le \frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}\sigma^{\alpha - \varepsilon} \end{equation*} \] This argument clearly also extends to \(1\le \sigma\le M\), given that the condition of Potter’s Bound, requiring that for \(t= 1/\theta\) and \(x = \sigma\) \[ \begin{equation*} 1/\theta \ge \max\cbr{t_0 t_0/\sigma} \ge t_0 \end{equation*} \] can always be made to hold as \(\theta\downarrow 0\) (fundamentally equivalent to Theorem 2). In their work they observe the fact that \[ \begin{equation*} \abs{\int_{0}^{\theta\lambda(\varepsilon)}e^{i\sigma}\frac{\Fbar(\sigma/\theta)}{\Fbar(1/\theta)} \dd \sigma} \le \frac{\theta\lambda(\varepsilon)}{\Fbar(1/\theta)} = o(1), \quad \theta\uparrow\infty, \end{equation*} \] These facts plus uniform convergence over compact \(1\le\sigma\le M\) allows them to derive a commensurate complex Karamata’s Tauberian Theorem.

Theorem 6 Let \(\mu\) be a probability distribution strictly supported on \(\R_+\) with \(S_1 \sim \mu\) and \(\Pr[S_1> n]=\ell(n)n^{-\alpha}\) for \(\alpha > 0\). Suppose that \(\alpha\) can be decomposed as \(\alpha = n + \beta\), for \(n \in \cbr{0,1,2,\ldots}\) and \(\beta \in (0,1)\). Then the following are equivalent:

  1. \(\Fbar(n) = \ell(n)n^{-\alpha}, \quad n\uparrow\infty\),
  2. \((-1)^{n+1}\left[\Phi (\theta) - \sum_{i=0}^{n}\frac{\E[S_1^j](i\theta)^{j}}{j!}\right] \sim e^{-\frac{i\pi\alpha}{2}}\abs{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\abs{\theta}^{\alpha}\ell(1/\abs{\theta}), \quad \theta\downarrow 0.\)

Specifically, for \(\alpha \in (0,1)\), \[ \begin{equation*} 1- \Phi(\theta) \sim e^{-\frac{i\pi\alpha}{2}}\abs{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\abs{\theta}^{\alpha}\ell(1/\abs{\theta}) , \quad \theta \downarrow 0, \end{equation*} \] and for \(\alpha \in (1,2)\), \[ \begin{equation*} (1 - \Phi(\theta)) +i\theta\E[ S_1] \sim -e^{-\frac{i\pi\alpha}{2}}\abs{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\abs{\theta}^{\alpha}\ell(1/\abs{\theta}) , \quad \theta \downarrow 0. \end{equation*} \]

Consider a probability generating function \(\mu(z) = \sum_{k \ge 1 } \mu_k z^k\) such that \(\Fbar(m) = \sum_{k>m}\mu_k = \ell(m)m^{-\alpha}\) for \(\alpha\in (0,1)\). Then, with \(z = e^{i\theta }\) for \(\theta >0\) , noting that \(-i\theta \approx 1 - z\) for small \(\theta\), Theorem 6 is equivalent to \[ \begin{equation} 1 -\mu(z) \sim \Gamma(1-\alpha)~ \ell\pr{ \frac{1}{\abs{1-z}}} \pr{1-z}^{\alpha} \quad z \uparrow 1, \end{equation} \tag{2}\] where we note that \((\theta)^\alpha \approx (-i\theta)^\alpha = e^{-\frac{i\pi \alpha}{2}}\theta^\alpha\) for \(\theta > 0\) as \(\theta\downarrow 0\). Using \(z\) in this way, rather than \(\theta\), is the statement of Karamata’s Tauberian Theorem (Karamata 1930) that is more typical in the literature.

Similarly, to use this equivalence to estimate the probability distribution from a given generator, we need only divide by the factor of \(\Gamma(1-\alpha)\) on the right-hand side in Equation 2, and invert the argument. Explicitly, when \(1 - \mu(z)\) is regularly varying as in Equation 2, we have that the tail is also regularly varying, with \[ \begin{align*} \Fbar\pr{\frac{1}{\abs{1-z}} } &\sim \frac{\abs{1 - \mu(z)}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \quad z \uparrow 1. \end{align*} \] Here, with \(\abs{1-z}\sim 1/n\) as \(n\uparrow\infty\), the expression \[ \begin{align*} \Fbar(n) &\sim \frac{\abs{1 - \mu\pr{1-\frac{1}{n}}}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \quad n \uparrow \infty, \end{align*} \] indicates directly that \(1-\mu(z)\) as \(\abs{1-z}\downarrow 0\) behaves inversely to \(\Fbar(n)\) as \(n\uparrow\infty\).

Informal proof of Karamata’s Tauberian Theorem

We begin by proving the only-if direction of the traditional version of Karamata’s Tauberian Theorem (for Laplace-Stieltjes transforms) for probability measures such that the tail \(\Fbar(m) = \ell(n)n^{-\alpha}\) is regularly varying with \(\alpha \in (0,1)\). 7

7 We choose the traditional version here for its simplicity, as it will only require us to cite Lemma 1. It is true however that Lemma 1 can be extended to complex \(k_\theta(x) = e^{i\theta x}\), where \(\int_0^\infty k_\theta(x) \Fbar(x) \dd x\) may not actually be absolutely integrable. This is again demonstrated in Lemma 3.2.1 of (Garsia and Lamperti 1963).

Proof. Here we prove the only-if direction of Theorem 6, focusing on the case of discrete distribution \(\mu\). See Theorem 1.7.1 in (Bingham et al. 1987) for an alternative full proof. By assumption, the survival function \(\Fbar(n) = \Pr[S_1 >n] = \ell(n)n^{-\alpha}\), is regularly varying. We will use Abel Summation to express our generating function directly in terms of this tail. First, consider a truncation to the first \(n\) terms which we will take the limit of \[ \begin{equation*} \int_{0}^{n} e^{-st} \dd F(t) = \sum_{1 \le k \le n} \mu_k e^{-sk} \end{equation*} \] written assuming that \(\mu_0 = 0\). We express the probability masses in terms of the tail as \[ \begin{equation*} \mu_n = \Pr[S_1 > n-1] - \Pr[S_1 > n] \doteq \Fbar(n-1) - \Fbar(n). \end{equation*} \] Using Abel Summation we may now write \[ \begin{align*} &\sum_{k=1}^n (\Fbar(k-1) - \Fbar(k)) e^{-sk} \\ &= e^{-s n}\sum_{1 \le k \le n} (\Fbar(k-1) - \Fbar(k)) - \int_{[1,n]} \dd (e^{-st}) \sum_{1 \le k \le \lfloor t\rfloor} (\Fbar(k-1) - \Fbar(k)) \end{align*} \] where, noting the summation is telescopic and that \(\Fbar(0) =1\), we have that \[ \begin{equation*} \sum_{1 \le k \le n} (\Fbar(k-1) - \Fbar(k)) = \Fbar(0) - \Fbar(n) = 1 - \Fbar(n). \end{equation*} \] We therefore write, with \(d\pr{e^{-st}} = -s e^{-st} \dd t\), \[ \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{n} e^{-st} \dd F(t) \\ &= \sum_{1 \le k \le n} \mu_k e^{-sk} \\ &= e^{-sn}(1 - \Fbar(n)) + s \int_{[1,n]}e^{-st}(1- \Fbar(\lfloor t \rfloor ))\dd t \\ &= e^{-sn} - e^{-sn}\Fbar(n) + (e^{-s} - e^{-sn}) - s\int_{[1,n]}e^{-st} \Fbar(\lfloor t \rfloor )\dd t \\ &= e^{-s} - e^{-sn}\Fbar(n) - s\int_{[1,n]}e^{-st} \Fbar(\lfloor t \rfloor )\dd t. \end{aligned} \end{equation} \tag{3}\]

For \(t \in (0,1)\), we have that \(\Fbar(\lfloor t \rfloor) = 1\) given our assumption that the associated random variable \(S_1 \in \Z_+\). Therefore, excluding the right endpoint, \[ \begin{align*} s\int_{(0,1)}e^{-st} \Fbar(\lfloor t \rfloor )\dd s &= s\int_{(0,1)}e^{-st} \dd t \\ &= 1 - e^{-s}. \end{align*} \] Thus we can rewrite Equation 3 over the entire interval \((0,n]\) as \[ \begin{equation} \int_{0}^{n} e^{-st} \dd F(t)= 1 - e^{-sn}\Fbar(n) - s \int_{(0,n]}e^{-st}\Fbar(\lfloor t \rfloor )\dd t \end{equation} \tag{4}\] From here, we consider the change of variables \(u = st\) in the integral expression in Equation 4 \[ \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{n} e^{-st} \dd F(t) % &= 1 - e^{-sn}\Fbar(n) - s \int_{(0,n]}e^{-st}\Fbar(\lfloor t \rfloor )\dd t \\ &= 1 - e^{-sn}\Fbar(n) - \int_{(0,n/s]}e^{-u}\Fbar(\lfloor u/s \rfloor )\dd u \end{align*} \] and lastly we will simply re-write the second term, hinting at our application of Lemma 1, as \[ \begin{equation*} \int_{0}^{n} e^{-st} \dd F(t)= 1 - e^{-sn}\Fbar(n) - \Fbar(1/s)\int_{(0,n/s]}e^{-u}\frac{\Fbar(\lfloor u/s \rfloor )}{\Fbar( 1/s )}\dd u \end{equation*} \] We now consider the truncated summation, for fixed \(s\), by sending \(n \uparrow \infty\). This eliminates the \(e^{-sn}\Fbar(n)\), and induces an integral over \(\R_+\), \[ \begin{equation} \lim_{n\uparrow\infty} \br{1 - e^{-sn}\Fbar(n) - \Fbar(1/s)\int_{(0,n/s]}e^{-u}\frac{\Fbar(\lfloor u/s \rfloor )}{\Fbar( 1/s )}\dd u }= 1 - \Fbar(1/s)\int_{(0,\infty)}e^{-u}\frac{\Fbar(\lfloor u/s \rfloor )}{\Fbar( 1/s )}\dd u \end{equation} \tag{5}\] By Lemma 1, taking \(k(u) = e^{-u}\) we have \[ \begin{equation*} \int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-u}\frac{\Fbar(\lfloor u/s \rfloor )}{\Fbar(\lfloor 1/s \rfloor )}\dd u = \int_{0}^{\infty}(1+ o(1))e^{-u}u^{-\alpha}\dd u = \int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-u}u^{-\alpha}\dd u + o(1) \rightarrow \Gamma(1-\alpha) < \infty, \quad s\downarrow 0. \end{equation*} \] Thus identifying Equation 5 with \(\Psi(s)\) as defined in the lemma statement, and applying the asymptotic statement above, we have \[ \begin{align*} 1 - \Psi(s) &= \Fbar(1/s)\int_{(0,\infty)}e^{-u}\frac{\Fbar(\lfloor u/s \rfloor )}{\Fbar( 1/s )}\dd u\\ &\sim \Gamma(1-\alpha)\Fbar(1/s), \quad s \downarrow 0 \\ &\sim \Gamma(1-\alpha) \ell(1/s)s^{\alpha} \end{align*} \] where the last line comes from the assumption that \(\Fbar\) is regularly varying with \(\Fbar(1/s) = \ell(1/s)s^{\alpha}\).

We now prove the extension of Theorem 6 to \(\alpha > 1\). It was not written in the context of, but this semi-proof is essentially what is provided in (Nair et al. 2022). Again this proof is done in the context of a Laplace-Stieltjes transform rather than a Fourier.

Proof. For \(n=0\), consider that by by Theorem 6 \[ \begin{equation*} g(x) = \int_{0}^{x}\Fbar(y) \dd y \end{equation*} \] has Laplace-Stieltjes transform after integration by parts which can be expressed as \[ \begin{equation} \hat{g}(s) = \frac{1}{s}\pr{1-\Psi(s)} \in \calR_{\alpha-1}^{0}. \end{equation} \tag{6}\] where \(\Psi(s)\) is the Laplace-Stieltjes transform of \(F\). For \(n =1\), i.e. \(-2 <\alpha < -1\) the idea is to consider an iterated integral over the proper ranges as presented in Karamata’s Theorem (Theorem 3), where for some \(t_0 \ge 0\) such that \(G(x)\) is bounded for finite \(x\), \[ \begin{equation} G(x) = \int_{t_0}^{x}\pr{\int_{z}^{\infty}\Fbar(y) \dd y} \dd z \sim \frac{-1}{(2-\alpha)(1-\alpha )}x^2 \Fbar(x) \in \calR_{2-\alpha}^{\infty}. \end{equation} \tag{7}\] Via integration by parts, provided \(\Pr[X\ge 0] = 1\), we have that \[ \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-st} \dd G(t) &= \int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-st} \pr{\int_{t}^{\infty}\Fbar(y) \dd y} \dd t \\ &= -\frac{1}{s}\pr{\int_{0}^{\infty}\Fbar(y) \dd y} + \frac{1}{s}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-st} \Fbar(t) \dd t \\ &= -\frac{1}{s}\E[X] + \frac{1}{s}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-st} \Fbar(t) \dd t \end{align*} \] noting that \(\E[X] = \int_{0}^{\infty}\Fbar(y) \dd y < \infty\). Using the substitution presented in Equation 6 \[ \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-st} \dd G(t) &= -\frac{1}{s}\E[S_1] + \frac{1}{s^2}\pr{1-\Psi(s)} \end{align*} \] Finally, per Equation 7, is due to the standard Karamata-Tauberian Theorem, Theorem (Theorem 6, for \(\alpha \in (0,1)\)), we have that \[ \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-st} \dd G(t) &= -\frac{1}{s}\E[S_1] + \frac{1}{s^2}\pr{1-\Psi(s)} \\ &\sim -\frac{\Gamma(3-\alpha)}{\Gamma(2-\alpha)\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\ell(1/s)s^{\alpha-2}. \end{align*} \] Multiplying across by \(s^{2}\) and re-arranging the expression, and recognizing that by the reflection principle for the \(\Gamma\)-function, we can define \[ \begin{equation*} -\frac{\Gamma(3-\alpha)}{(2-\alpha)(1-\alpha )} \doteq \abs{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}. \end{equation*} \] completes our intended portion of the proof. We note additionally, as Weirmann et al. (page 47 of Nair et al. (2022)) point out, the reverse direction of the proof indicating the behavior of \(\Fbar(n)\) is a simple result of the Monotone Density Theorem (Theorem 1) where by construction \(G(x)\) is monotone.

Extending this to the Fourier Transform case amounts to simply inserting back the definition of \(s = -i\theta\) in the integration by parts carried out, and adjusting the constant in front of the regular varying term..
